summary: Defines full-mode fax carriage over the Internet using Internet mail, building on earlier simple-mode work. It adds the functionality needed for reliable, confirmed delivery comparable to classic fax. This is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Old fax machines tell you when your page really arrived. This memo gives email-based faxing the same kind of receipts and checks, so you know it got there.

questions: what is full mode internet fax
how does internet fax negotiate capabilities
why does fax over email need direct mode
subtitle: Closing the gap between email-based fax and classic fax with content negotiation and richer TIFF.

tldr.problem: Classic fax lets the sender learn what the receiver can handle before sending. Internet mail is store-and-forward with potentially long latency, so that kind of before-the-fact negotiation is hard.
tldr.mechanism: FFPIM builds on the simple and extended fax-over-mail profiles. It requires content negotiation through a post-hoc user agent mechanism, allows an ESMTP-based mechanism, and adds enhanced TIFF data.
tldr.outcome: Email-based fax can approximate the service level of classic T.30 fax using standard mail infrastructure, but negotiation brings security risks such as denial of service and information disclosure.

today: RFC 4142 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines full mode carriage of facsimile data over the Internet. It builds on RFC 3965 (a simple mode of fax using Internet mail) and RFC 2532 (extended facsimile using Internet mail). Implementations that conform to it MUST also conform to both.

The goal is a level of service that closely approximates what fax users enjoy, using the existing mail infrastructure. Where possible the new features reuse standard email mechanisms, such as positive delivery confirmation and disposition notification, instead of fax-specific features that non-fax software is unlikely to implement. Terminology is covered in RFC 2542.
sections.eli5: Full mode is the upgrade that makes sending a fax by email work more like a real fax machine, while still using normal email.

sections.title: Content Negotiation
sections.content:
Classic fax is interactive: the sending station discovers the receiver's capabilities and sends the best quality both support. Internet mail is store-and-forward with potentially long latency, so before-the-fact negotiation is problematic. Without some mechanism, a sender cannot be certain the receiver supports a richer document form than the safer-but-universal default.

The capabilities that can be negotiated are specified in RFC 2534 and RFC 2879. FFPIM implementations MUST support content negotiation as described there.
sections.eli5: The sender wants to know whether the receiver can handle the fancy version of a page. Since email is slow, they need clever ways to find out.

sections.title: Two Ways to Negotiate
sections.content:
UA-based negotiation is a post-hoc technique specified in RFC 3297. The originator sends the best version known to be supported by the recipient, and also sends a better suited version if the recipient asks for it. FFPIM implementations MUST support this mechanism.

ESMTP-based negotiation uses an ESMTP option specified in RFC 4141. It needs support for content negotiation along the entire path the email travels. Receiving servers can report the capabilities of the mailboxes they support, and sending clients can signal permission and constraints on conversions. FFPIM participants MAY support this mechanism.

The two mechanisms must be used compatibly. They might consult different repositories of capabilities information that disagree, which means at least one is inaccurate, so the larger problem is correctness rather than synchronization. The RFC does not require a particular way of using them together.
sections.eli5: One way is to send a good copy first and a better copy if the receiver asks. The other is to ask the receiver's mail server what it can read before sending.

sections.title: Content Format
sections.content:
FFPIM allows the transfer of enhanced TIFF data relative to RFC 3965 and RFC 2532. The details are in RFC 3949, and conformant implementations SHOULD support the TIFF enhancements.

Because negotiation lets a sender learn the full range of content types the recipient supports, the TIFF support requirements are a functional minimum for FFPIM.
sections.eli5: Fax pages are sent as a kind of picture file called TIFF. Full mode allows fancier versions of those picture files.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security sections of RFC 3965 and RFC 2532 apply, including PGP and S/MIME use for authentication and privacy. The new mechanisms appear not to introduce new security considerations, though the concerns in RFC 2532 are particularly salient. Three are listed:

  • Negotiation can be used as a denial of service attack.
  • Negotiation may lead to the use of an unsafe data format.
  • Negotiation discloses information and so raises privacy concerns.

The ESMTP option permits content transformation by an intermediary. Encrypted content cannot be converted because the intermediary lacks the keys, and converting signed content invalidates the signature. Permission to convert SHOULD NOT normally be used with signed or sealed messages. The RFC also notes that allowing conversion by unspecified intermediaries carries significant risk and points to RFC 3238.
sections.eli5: Asking questions about what someone can read also tells others things about them. And if a helper changes your letter on the way, a signature that proved it was yours stops working.

sections.title: Direct Mode
sections.content:
Fax is generally considered direct and immediate, while email has highly variable delay and an unknown number of relays. Fully emulating fax means faithful document semantics and a timely interaction like telephony-based fax. FFPIM and its predecessors cover the first. The ESMTP option sets the stage for the second, but timeliness needs sender and receiver mail servers to talk directly.

To send directly, the originating MTA must not use sending-side intermediaries such as outbound enterprise MTAs, and must deliver straight to hosts named in addresses using the public DNS. To receive directly, target MTAs must have DNS A records without MX records. With typical configurations the content and interaction semantics can be emulated well, but timeliness cannot be assured.
sections.eli5: For a real-time chat like a fax call, the two mail computers must talk straight to each other with no stops in between.
